chunks: "Synchronous rectification means replacing the buck's freewheel diode with a second MOSFET on the low side.
It's driven opposite to the high-side FET: when the high side is off, the low side turns on and carries the inductor current. The win is efficiency.
A diode has a fixed forward drop, 0. 3 to 0. 5 volts for a Schottky, so its loss is V f times I times the fraction of time it conducts.
A FET behaves like a resistor, so the loss is I squared R DS(on) . For 12 volts in, 3.
3 volts out and 2 amps, the Schottky wastes about 650 milliwatts and a 10 milliohms FET about 30 milliwatts.
The advantage grows as the output voltage falls, because the low side conducts more of the cycle, and the converter runs cooler. The cons are complexity and new failure modes.
You need a second gate driver and dead time so both FETs never conduct together; during that gap the body diode conducts and adds loss and reverse-recovery charge.
You pay gate-drive loss Q g V f for the extra FET even at no load.
And at light load, a fully synchronous bridge lets the inductor current go negative, which circulates energy for no benefit.
So controllers add diode emulation or PFM to turn the low side off when current reaches zero."
